title: Thales Corners the Olive Presses
text:
Thales of Miletus, often called the first Greek philosopher, lived in the 6th century BC. Aristotle, in his Politics, tells a story about him that was already old in Aristotle's time.

People mocked Thales for his poverty, saying it proved that philosophy was useless. According to the story, Thales used his knowledge of the heavens to foresee, while it was still winter, that the coming olive harvest would be exceptionally large. With the little money he had, he paid small deposits to rent all the olive presses in Miletus and on the island of Chios. Because it was winter and no one else was bidding, he got them cheaply.

When harvest time came, everyone suddenly needed presses at once. Thales controlled them all and rented them out on whatever terms he chose. He made a large sum of money. Aristotle says Thales thus showed that it is easy for philosophers to become rich if they want to, but that wealth is not what they care about.

Aristotle himself adds a dry comment: the method was not really a matter of special wisdom but a general principle of making money, which is to create a monopoly. Some cities, he notes, used the same trick when they needed funds.
lesson: Foresight pays most when you act on it early and cheaply, before others see what you see. Secure your position while it costs little.
caveat: Aristotle presents it as a traditional story about Thales, so it may be legend.
